title: Expressivity and Universality
intro: Which input-output maps a quantum reservoir with a linear readout can approximate: universality for fading-memory filters, the polynomial structure that the input encoding imposes, and hard bounds from feature rank and capacity.

blocks.text: The function class: fading-memory filters

A reservoir maps an input sequence $(\dots, s_{k-1}, s_k)$ to an output $\hat y_k$. The natural target class is the causal, time-invariant filters with fading memory: $y_k = G(s_k, s_{k-1}, s_{k-2}, \dots)$ where inputs far in the past matter less and less. Formally, with a decreasing weight sequence $\lambda_j \to 0$, $G$ is continuous in the weighted norm $\sup_j \lambda_j |s_{k-j}|$. Boyd and Chua showed that every such filter on bounded inputs is uniformly approximated by a finite Volterra series, a polynomial in finitely many past inputs:

blocks.tex: y_k \approx h_0 + \sum_{j} h_1(j)\, s_{k-j} + \sum_{j \le l} h_2(j,l)\, s_{k-j} s_{k-l} + \dots
blocks.caption: A truncated Volterra series: the benchmark class for what a reservoir should reach.

blocks.text: So the expressivity question splits in two. Memory: how far back $j$ can the reservoir reach, which is set by contraction (the echo state property). Nonlinearity: which monomials, and of what degree, can a linear readout of its features form. A classical echo state network gets both from $\tanh$ and a spectral radius below about one; a quantum reservoir gets memory from dissipation and nonlinearity from somewhere less obvious, because quantum mechanics is linear in $\rho$.
Where nonlinearity comes from when the dynamics are linear

The channel acts linearly on $\rho$, and the features are linear in $\rho$. The only route for nonlinearity in $s$ is the dependence of the channel on the input. For the reset (state-injection) encoding of Input Encoding (#/qrc/models/input-encoding), qubit 1 is replaced by $\vert\psi(s)\rangle = \sqrt{1-s}\vert 0\rangle + \sqrt{s}\vert 1\rangle$, whose density matrix has entries $1-s$, $s$ and $\sqrt{s(1-s)}$. The whole step is therefore an affine combination of three fixed channels:

blocks.caption: Each $\mathcal{T}_m$ is a fixed linear map; $\mathcal{T}_0$ is the channel for $s = 0$, while $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ are not channels on their own. $\mathcal{T}_s$ is CPTP for every $s \in [0,1]$.

blocks.text: Unrolling $L$ steps and replacing the state $L$ steps back by a fixed state $\rho_*$ gives the reservoir's own Volterra-like expansion:

blocks.caption: With $g_0 = 1$, $g_1(s) = s$, $g_2(s) = \sqrt{s(1-s)}$. The error is exponentially small in $L$ when the channel contracts.

blocks.text: Read the structure off this sum. Every output is a sum of products across time, each factor drawn from $\mathrm{span}\{1, s, \sqrt{s(1-s)}\}$ of one past input. Cross-time products such as $s_k s_{k-1}$ come for free (they are terms with two non-trivial factors). But the dependence on any single input is confined to a three-dimensional function space, however many qubits or virtual nodes you add. The target $s_k^2$ is outside that span and can only be approximated, through $\sqrt{s(1-s)}$; the sample in Hands-on Implementation (#/qrc/theory/hands-on-implementation) measures the best possible NMSE inside the span as 0.0018 on its test set (0.0020 exactly for uniform $s$) and a 4-qubit reservoir with 40 features at 0.0113.

This is the quantum counterpart of a classical fact: a linear reservoir driven additively by the input can only produce a linear filter. Nonlinearity in a quantum reservoir is a property of the encoding (and of the readout), not of the Hamiltonian. A richer Hamiltonian changes which combinations of the monomials are reachable and how well conditioned they are, not which monomials exist.
Ways to enrich the encoding

items: Upload the same input more than once. Writing $s_k$ into two qubits gives $c(s) \otimes c(s)$ with $c(s) = (1, s, \sqrt{s(1-s)})$, whose span is $\{1, s, \sqrt{s(1-s)}, s^2, s\sqrt{s(1-s)}\}$: five functions, now including $s^2$. With $r$ copies the per-input degree grows linearly in $r$. This is the time-series version of data re-uploading.

Encode in an angle. A rotation $e^{-i\theta s X/2}$ makes the state depend on $\cos(\theta s)$ and $\sin(\theta s)$, so each use contributes frequencies $\{0, \pm\theta\}$; $r$ uses give a truncated Fourier series with frequencies up to $r\theta$ (Schuld, Sweke and Meyer). The spectrum is fixed by the encoding generator's eigenvalue differences, and the reservoir only sets the coefficients.

Encode in the Hamiltonian. Driving a field $h(s)$ for time $\tau$ gives $e^{-i(H_0 + s H_1)\tau}$, whose dependence on $s$ contains all eigenvalue differences of $H_0 + sH_1$, a much richer (and harder to analyse) function class.

Make the readout nonlinear. Products of measured features $x_{k,i}x_{k,j}$ are not linear in $\rho_k$ but are linear in $\rho_k \otimes \rho_k$, the state of two copies. Polynomial readouts are the cheapest classical route to the missing degree; the price is that the readout is no longer what makes the quantum system interesting.

blocks.text: Universality: the Stone–Weierstrass route

Many universality theorems for reservoirs follow one template, which goes back to Boyd and Chua's Volterra-series result and was carried to dissipative qubit networks by Chen and Nurdin. (Grigoryeva and Ortega proved that echo state networks themselves are universal by a different route, through the topology of the fading-memory property and approximation of the reservoir map.) Consider a family $\mathcal{F}$ of reservoir-plus-readout filters. If (i) every member has the echo state property and fading memory, (ii) $\mathcal{F}$ contains the constants, (iii) $\mathcal{F}$ separates points (two input histories that differ give different outputs for some member) and (iv) $\mathcal{F}$ is closed under addition and multiplication, then by Stone–Weierstrass on the compact space of input sequences $\mathcal{F}$ is dense in the fading-memory filters.
Quantum mechanics hands you closure under products almost for free. Run two reservoirs side by side; the joint state is $\rho^{(1)}_k \otimes \rho^{(2)}_k$, and

blocks.caption: Products of outputs are outputs of the product reservoir.

blocks.text: Sums are a linear readout over the disjoint union of the two reservoirs. So the hard parts are (i) and (iii): contraction for every input, and separation. Chen and Nurdin proved universality in this sense for a class of dissipative qubit-network reservoirs; Nokkala and co-authors did so for Gaussian continuous-variable reservoirs with suitable readouts. Martínez-Peña and Ortega gave conditions for the echo state and fading-memory properties of finite-dimensional quantum reservoirs, including when contraction holds for every input.

Universality is existence, not efficiency. The theorem says some member of the family, of some size, approximates the target; it says nothing about how many qubits, how many observables or how many shots that takes. Every practical limit on this shelf lives in that gap.
Hard bounds: feature rank and capacity

Features are linear functionals of $\rho_k$, and $\rho_k$ lives in the real vector space of Hermitian $2^n \times 2^n$ matrices with unit trace, which has dimension $4^n - 1$. Hence at any time step at most $4^n - 1$ features are linearly independent, no matter how many observables or virtual nodes are read. Time multiplexing (virtual nodes) reads $\rho$ at $V$ sub-steps; it adds independent features only until it reaches the dimension of the set of states the reservoir actually visits, which is often far smaller than $4^n - 1$.

Capacity is bounded by the same count. Jaeger showed that the linear memory capacity $\mathrm{MC} = \sum_{d \ge 1} r^2(d)$ of a reservoir with $N$ readout features driven by i.i.d. input is at most $N$; Dambre and co-authors extended this to the total information-processing capacity summed over all orthogonal polynomial targets of the past inputs, which is also at most $N$ and reaches $N$ exactly for a fading-memory system whose features are linearly independent. For a quantum reservoir $N$ is the number of linearly independent features, so

blocks.caption: Total capacity is budgeted: memory and nonlinearity draw on the same $N_{\text{eff}}$.

blocks.text: The budget explains the memory–nonlinearity trade-off seen in every reservoir: capacity spent on reproducing old inputs linearly is not available for products, and vice versa. With finite shots the budget shrinks further, because a feature whose input-driven variance is below the shot-noise variance contributes almost nothing; see Concentration and Scalability (#/qrc/theory/concentration-and-scalability).

widget.title: A product target exposes the cross-time terms

blocks.text: Try the product task first: with the default 4 qubits and $V = 5$ the reservoir predicts $s_k s_{k-1}$ well, because cross-time products are native to the expansion above. Then set $V = 1$ (4 features) and watch NMSE rise: the products are still in the span, but four features cannot hold them together with the linear terms. Switch to NARMA2 and raise $V$ to 10 to see NMSE fall to roughly half its $V = 5$ value. Finally add shots (1000) and watch the fit degrade, though the function class has not changed.
Worked problems

blocks.title: Feature rank of a three-qubit reservoir
blocks.text: A 3-qubit reservoir is read out through $\langle Z_i\rangle$ at $V$ virtual nodes. Above what $V$ can the extra virtual nodes no longer add linearly independent features, whatever the dynamics?
blocks.hint: Count the real dimension of unit-trace Hermitian matrices.
solution: Features are linear in $\rho_k$, which lies in the affine space of unit-trace Hermitian $8 \times 8$ matrices.
That space has real dimension $4^3 - 1 = 63$, so at most 63 independent features exist (plus the constant, which the readout bias supplies).

Each virtual node adds $n = 3$ features, so $3V \le 63$ gives $V \le 21$. From $V = 22$ on, extra nodes are linearly dependent on earlier ones; in practice the reachable set is smaller and saturation comes sooner.

blocks.title: What a second upload buys
blocks.text: With reset encoding each use of the input contributes $c(s) = (1, s, \sqrt{s(1-s)})$. If $s_k$ is written into two qubits at the same step, what is the dimension of the space of single-input functions the reservoir can now form?
blocks.hint: Expand $(1, s, r)\otimes(1, s, r)$ with $r^2 = s(1-s)$.
solution: The step depends on $s$ through the products of entries of $c(s) \otimes c(s)$: $1, s, \sqrt{s(1-s)}, s^2, s\sqrt{s(1-s)}$ and $\sqrt{s(1-s)}^2 = s - s^2$.
The last is a combination of $s$ and $s^2$, and the cross terms repeat, so the distinct span is $\{1, s, \sqrt{s(1-s)}, s^2, s\sqrt{s(1-s)}\}$.
These five functions are linearly independent on $[0,1]$.

blocks.title: Capacity budget
blocks.text: A 4-qubit reservoir with $V = 5$ reads 20 features. Its linear memory capacity (delays 1 to 12) is measured at 3.86. If its features are linearly independent and it has fading memory, how much capacity is left for nonlinear targets of past inputs, at most?
solution: The total information-processing capacity over all orthogonal targets is at most the number of independent features, here 20 (with equality for a fading-memory system with independent features).
Linear memory already uses 3.86; the delay-0 recall ($r^2 \approx 1$) is also a linear target and uses about 1 more.
That leaves at most about $20 - 3.86 - 1 \approx 15$ for nonlinear targets (products, squares, higher degrees), shared among all of them.
